steps.body: Here's a multiplication secret: 3 × 4 and 4 × 3 give the **same total**. An array shows why — build 3 rows of 4 dots, then turn the page sideways. Now it reads 4 rows of 3. Same dots. Nothing appeared, nothing vanished.
Build an array that still works when it turns.

widget.prompt: Build a 2-by-5 array. The same 10 squares can also be read as 5 by 2 when the array turns.
widget.factorFeedback: The area is 10, but use side lengths 2 and 5 so the turn shows 2 × 5 and 5 × 2.
widget.lowFeedback: The array has fewer than 10 squares. Make one side 2 and the other 5.
widget.highFeedback: The array has more than 10 squares. Make one side 2 and the other 5.
widget.successFeedback: The 2-by-5 and 5-by-2 views contain the same 10 squares. Turning the array changes the viewpoint, not the total.

predict.prompt: Turn a 2 × 5 array on its side and it reads 5 × 2. Does the dot count change?

options.label: Yes — there are more rows now

predict.reveal: Rotating rearranges nothing: the same 10 dots are just read as 5 columns of 2. That's the whole proof that 2 × 5 = 5 × 2 — every fact you learn buys its twin for free.

steps.body: A fact and its flip are **twins**.
explanationVariants: 3 × 6 is 6 × 3 turned sideways — same dots, same total: 18.
6 rows of 3 flipped becomes 3 rows of 6. Count either way and you get 18.

widget.prompt: Which fact always has the SAME total as 6 × 3?

options.feedback: The flip! 6 × 3 and 3 × 6 are the same array turned sideways — both make 18.
6 + 3 = 9 joins the numbers once. 6 × 3 makes six whole groups of 3 — that's 18, twice as much.
6 × 6 = 36 changes a number instead of flipping. A flip keeps BOTH numbers, just in the other order.
3 × 3 = 9 drops the 6 entirely. Flipping keeps both numbers: 6 and 3 stay, only their order swaps.

steps.body: Why care? Because you get to **pick the easier direction**. Solving 9 × 2 the long way means nine hops of 2. Flip it to 2 × 9 and it's just two hops: 9, 18. Same answer, way less counting.
Flip, then hop the short way.
explanationVariants: Flip 9 × 2 into 2 × 9: two hops of 9 — 9, then 18.
9 × 2 means nine 2s: 2, 4, 6, 8, 10, 12, 14, 16, 18. The flip gets there in two hops instead.

widget.prompt: Leo has to solve 9 × 2. He flips it to 2 × 9 and counts two hops of 9. What is 9 × 2?

commonErrors.feedback: 11 adds 9 + 2. Multiplying makes 9 groups of 2 (or 2 groups of 9) — more than one join.
92 writes the digits side by side. Hop instead: 9, then 9 more.
81 is 9 × 9 — the 2 got lost in the flip. Flipping keeps both numbers: 2 × 9.

widget.fallbackFeedback: Take the short direction: two hops of 9. Say them: 9, then 18.

steps.body: Every fact has exactly one **flip twin**.

widget.prompt: Match each fact to its turned-around twin.

pairErrors.feedback: 2 × 4 is the twin of 4 × 2, not of 3 × 5. A twin swaps a fact's OWN two numbers — 3 × 5 flips to 5 × 3.

widget.missFeedback: A twin keeps the same two numbers and only swaps their order. Match each fact to the one using its exact numbers.
widget.successFeedback: Every fact found its twin — same numbers, opposite order, identical totals.

steps.body: Either direction earns full credit — the array doesn't care which way you read it.
explanationVariants: 7 rows of 3 stars can be written 7 × 3 — or flipped to 3 × 7. Both count the same 21 stars.
Read it rows-first (7 × 3) or turn the poster sideways (3 × 7). The stars never move: 21 either way.

widget.prompt: A poster shows 7 rows with 3 stars in each row. Build a multiplication for the total stars — either direction counts!

commonBuilds.feedback: 7 + 3 joins the numbers once and makes 10. The poster holds 7 whole rows of 3 — equal groups need ×.

widget.missFeedback: Use both of the poster's numbers — 7 and 3 — joined by ×, in either order.
widget.successFeedback: Yes — and its flip works too. 7 × 3 = 3 × 7 = 21 stars.

steps.body: Use the flip to unlock a fact you already know.
hints: Sam already knows 4 × 6 = 24. Look closely at 6 × 4 — how is it related?
6 × 4 is the flip of 4 × 6, so it's also 24. That handles the first part.
Now finish the problem: take that 24 and add the 10 extra stickers.
explanationVariants: Flip 6 × 4 into the known fact 4 × 6 = 24, then add the extras: 24 + 10 = 34.
The flip says 6 × 4 = 24 without any new counting. Ten more stickers brings the pile to 34.

widget.prompt: Sam knows 4 × 6 = 24 but hasn't learned his 6-times table. He gets 6 packs of 4 stickers, plus 10 loose stickers. How many stickers in all?

commonErrors.feedback: 24 covers the packs — the flip worked! But 10 loose stickers are still on the table. Add them in.
20 adds 6 + 4 + 10. The packs are equal groups: 6 packs of 4 is 6 × 4, which flips to 4 × 6 = 24.
240 tacks the 10 on as a zero. The 10 loose stickers get ADDED to 24, not glued onto it.

widget.fallbackFeedback: Two steps: flip 6 × 4 into 4 × 6 (which Sam knows), then add the 10 loose stickers.

steps.body: You just cut the times table in half.
takeaways: Flipping the two numbers never changes the total — the array only turns sideways.
Flip to whichever direction is easier to count.
Order changes the story (6 packs of 4 ≠ 4 packs of 6) but never the total.
steps.teaser: make the ×2, ×5 and ×10 facts automatic — with tricks, not memorizing.

concept.body: Quick rewind. Build any array and **turn it sideways**: 2 rows of 5 becomes 5 rows of 2. No dot appears or disappears, so 2 × 5 = 5 × 2. Flipping the two numbers in a multiplication never changes the answer.

explanationVariants: Five 2s and two 5s count the same dots: 10.

options.feedback: The flip — same two numbers, other order, same total of 10.
5 + 2 = 7 joins once. 5 × 2 makes five groups of 2 — that's 10.
5 × 5 swaps the 2 for another 5. A flip keeps both original numbers.
